A 2021 analysis of 120 industrial hydrogen incidents showed that pipe rupture and fitting/valve breakdown are the main causes of hydrogen leaks, while human error related to incorrect part disassembly, assembly, movement, and replacement contributed significantly as well [12]. Likewise, in 2022, researchers evaluated incidents from the Hydrogen Incidents and Accidents Database (HIAD) 2.0 database and concluded that half of all events were related to organizational and management errors such as poor planning, lack of safety systems/barriers, poor communication 11 (especially with contractors), and carelessness, while the second main cause was material and manufacturing failures [13]. These studies emphasize the importance of consistent performance of proper maintenance, component integrity, and the avoidance of pipe or tank rupture. Existing regulations play an important role in developing safety protocols for hydrogen rail and maintenance facilities. A safety codes and standards analysis conducted in 2024 revealed that existing regulations are largely applicable to hydrogen rail maintenance facilities, however, many requirements, including those in NFPA 2, could be reviewed to assess their applicability for larger systems in enclosed spaces, such as hydrogen rail cars in maintenance facilities [14]. These FMEA, HAZOP, and code analysis findings, together with the information presented in this report, can collectively enable more focused and cost-effective design and operation of maintenance facilities for hydrogen rail. 1.1. Unique factors associated with hydrogen rail in maintenance facilities There are unique technical and design aspects which need to be considered in hydrogen rail maintenance facility hazard analysis which may be different from typical hazards found in a non- hydrogen rail maintenance facility. These hydrogen-specific hazards were used to help inform this qualitative risk analysis to enable the identification of the most severe operational hazards and to prescribe effective countermeasures for their avoidance. Though fuel tanks for diesel and diesel electric trains may be serviced in a maintenance facility, if fuel tank service is performed for a hydrogen locomotive, there are unique potential hazards which should be considered including inadequate defueling of the tank prior to service. This involves the unintended release of 35 MPa or 70 MPa pressurized hydrogen or liquid hydrogen. These are important considerations since the flammability limits of hydrogen at normal atmospheric pressure are 4 vol% to 75 vol% in air [15]. Also, the minimum ignition energy is comparatively very low (0.02 mJ), requiring much lower ignition energy than diesel-air mixtures [15]. This highlights the importance of preventing the release of hydrogen and its accumulation in enclosed facilities, especially for hydrogen tanks on railcars or tenders, due to the large amount of hydrogen onboard. Since the unintended release of hundreds of kilograms of hydrogen in an enclosed space is possible, and due to the potential for fire or delayed explosion, this was a primary hazardous scenario considered in this analysis.
